messages.name: Nathan
messages.subject: Mobile mapping route planning
messages.thought: I emailed Paul earlier today, but wanted to reach out to you too since you're closer to the ML side at Aclima. Reading about the mobile mapping work, I got interested in the route-planning problem; with limited driving time, where you send the cars changes what you get to observe and what you miss.
messages.work: That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on for that kind of real-world impact. One idea would be to simulate different routing strategies under the same driving budget and test whether smarter route selection improves the resulting map, but I'd rather shape it around whatever planning problem would actually be useful to the team.
messages.body:
Hi Nathan,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I emailed Paul earlier today, but wanted to reach out to you too since you're closer to the ML side at Aclima. Reading about the mobile mapping work, I got interested in the route-planning problem; with limited driving time, where you send the cars changes what you get to observe and what you miss.

Lately I've been looking for ways to use more of my planning and ML work on problems with a real-world benefit, and this felt close enough to what I already do that I could be useful.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on for that kind of real-world impact. One idea would be to simulate different routing strategies under the same driving budget and test whether smarter route selection improves the resulting map, but I'd rather shape it around whatever planning problem would actually be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

One idea would be to test how gaps in vessel observations change the interpretation of a track or make its identity ambiguous, but I'd rather shape it around whatever problem would actually be useful to the research team.

messages.name: Josef
messages.subject: Forecast error and line ratings
messages.thought: I also emailed John earlier today, but wanted to reach out to you too since your team works directly on uncertainty in the weather inputs to LineVision's ratings. I got interested in how errors in wind or temperature forecasts carry through to the predicted line capacity, and when those errors become large enough to actually matter for the rating.
messages.motivation: Lately I've been looking for ways to use more of my planning and simulation work on problems with a real-world benefit, and getting more capacity out of existing grid infrastructure felt like a useful place to apply it.
messages.work: That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to simulate different levels of forecast error and test when they start materially changing the predicted rating, but I'd rather shape it around whatever question would actually be useful to the team.

messages.name: Kevin
messages.subject: Routing after delivery delays
messages.thought: I also emailed Scott earlier today, but wanted to reach out to you too given your operations research work. A lot of the planning work I'm doing is about recovering when the original plan stops being valid, which made me interested in the same problem in delivery routing; if one delivery runs late, how much of the remaining route actually needs to change to get the schedule back on track?
messages.motivation: Lately I've been looking for ways to use more of my planning work on problems with a real-world benefit, and this felt close enough to what I already do that I could be useful.
messages.work: That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to simulate delivery delays and compare replanning strategies based on how much lateness they recover and how much of the existing route they change, but I'd rather shape it around whatever routing problem would actually be useful to the team.
